"The actions of the Georgian authorities in South Ossetia are a crime, of course, primarily a crime against their own people," Putin said, according to Russian news agency Interfax. Meanwhile, Cheney talked to Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili on Sunday, telling him that Russia's aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered." Cheney's spokeswoman Lea Ann McBride said the vice president spoke to Saakashvili to express "the United States' solidarity with the Georgian people and their democratically elected government in the face of this threat to Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity." Georgia withdrew its forces Sunday and offered a ceasefire, which Russia refused. "The vice president told President Saakashvili that Russian aggression must not go unanswered, and that its continuation would have serious consequences for its relations with the United States, as well as the broader international community," McBride said. Saakashvili has called on the United States and the world community to stop the "intervention and invasion of my sovereign country." "I think the U.S. is the most powerful country in the world," he told CNN. "I think the U.S. has lots of leverage. And I think there are lots of diplomatic means that it could be done through." # Bush Condemns Escalating Violence Between Russia and Georgia

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush on Sunday condemned the intensifying conflict between Russia and its U.S.-backed neighbor Georgia, while Vice President Dick Cheney declared that Russian aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered."

Speaking from Beijing, where he was attending Olympic events, President Bush addressed the crisis in an interview with NBC's Bob Costas. "My administration has been engaged with both sides of this, trying to get a cease-fire," he said. Bush was captured on camera conversing with Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin during Friday's Olympic opening ceremonies, and he later confirmed that he had been direct with his Russian counterpart. "I was firm with Vladimir Putin," Bush said, adding, "This violence is unacceptable."

The conflict between Russia and its Western-allied neighbor has raged since Thursday, when Georgia launched a military operation to suppress separatists in the South Ossetia region. Russia maintains that its actions are intended to protect peacekeeping forces stationed in South Ossetia under prior cease-fire agreements. Georgia, however, has characterized Russia's response as a full-scale invasion.

The two nations have traded serious accusations: Russia contends that Georgia is pursuing a genocidal campaign to purge the region of ethnic Ossetians loyal to Moscow, while Georgia asserts that Russia is executing a long-premeditated war aimed at seizing control of the territory—including a strategically vital pipeline that transports Asian oil to Black Sea ports.

"I expressed my grave concern about the disproportionate response of Russia," Bush said, recounting his conversation with Putin. "We strongly condemn bombing outside of South Ossetia."

For his part, Putin voiced concern over the growing wave of refugees fleeing into Russia from South Ossetia. According to Russian news agency Interfax, Russian officials reported that more than 30,000 refugees crossed into Russia over the past two days. "The actions of the Georgian authorities in South Ossetia are a crime, of course, primarily a crime against their own people," Putin said, as quoted by Interfax.

Meanwhile, Cheney spoke by phone with Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili on Sunday, reinforcing that Russia's aggression "must not go unanswered." According to Cheney's spokeswoman, Lea Ann McBride, the vice president's call was intended to convey "the United States' solidarity with the Georgian people and their democratically elected government in the face of this threat to Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity."

Georgia withdrew its forces on Sunday and proposed a cease-fire, an offer that Russia rejected. "The vice president told President Saakashvili that Russian aggression must not go unanswered, and that its continuation would have serious consequences for its relations with the United States, as well as the broader international community," McBride stated.

Saakashvili, in turn, has appealed to the United States and the broader international community to halt what he described as the "intervention and invasion of my sovereign country." Speaking to CNN, he emphasized America's capacity to influence the situation: "I think the U.S. is the most powerful country in the world. I think the U.S. has lots of leverage. And I think there are lots of diplomatic means that it could be done through."

Two senior officials have confirmed to CNN that the United States has dispatched envoy Matt Bryza to the region to assist in mediation efforts.

# Escalating Crisis in the Caucasus: U.S. Response to Russia-Georgia Conflict

The Bush administration has taken a firm stance against the rapidly deteriorating situation in the Caucasus region, as violence between Russia and Georgia continues to escalate with no clear resolution in sight. President Bush publicly condemned the conflict, describing the situation as "unacceptable" and voicing serious alarm over what he characterized as Russia's "disproportionate response" to the crisis. His remarks signal growing concern within the administration that Moscow's military actions have far exceeded any reasonable justification, even accounting for Russia's stated aim of protecting its peacekeeping forces in the region.

Adding to the administration's show of support for Georgia, Vice President Dick Cheney placed a direct call to Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili. During their conversation, Cheney delivered a pointed warning, stating that Russian aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered." This statement represents one of the strongest expressions of U.S. solidarity with Tbilisi since the conflict erupted, underscoring Washington's concern that unchecked Russian military action could have broader implications for regional stability and international norms regarding sovereignty.

The roots of the current crisis trace back to Thursday, when Georgian forces launched a military operation targeting separatist fighters in South Ossetia, a breakaway region that has long sought independence from Georgian control. In response, Russia moved swiftly to intervene militarily, framing its actions as necessary to protect Russian peacekeepers stationed in the area. This rapid escalation from a localized conflict with separatists to a full-scale confrontation between two nations has alarmed international observers and raised fears of a broader regional war.

The two nations have since engaged in an intense war of narratives, each accusing the other of egregious misconduct. Russian officials have alleged that Georgia's military campaign amounted to a genocidal plot targeting ethnic Ossetians, framing Tbilisi's actions as an attempt at ethnic cleansing. Georgia, for its part, has countered these claims by asserting that Russia's intervention was not a spontaneous response to protect peacekeepers, but rather the execution of a long-premeditated war strategy designed to assert control over South Ossetia and, by extension, the strategically vital oil pipeline routes that traverse the region.

The humanitarian toll of the conflict has grown increasingly severe. Russian officials have reported that more than 30,000 refugees fled South Ossetia into Russian territory within just two days, highlighting the rapid deterioration of conditions on the ground and the widespread displacement caused by the fighting. As the situation continues to unfold, the international community faces mounting pressure to intervene diplomatically before the conflict escalates further, with competing narratives and accusations from both sides complicating efforts to broker a ceasefire or lasting resolution.

**Bush Condemns Russian Military Action in Georgia, Demands Withdrawal**

*CNN*

WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Bush issued a sharp condemnation of Russia's military operations in Georgia on Monday, calling for an immediate end to the violence and demanding that Russian forces withdraw from the breakaway region of South Ossetia and Georgian territory.

Speaking from the White House, Bush said the United States stood firmly behind Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity, warning that Russia's actions threatened to isolate it from the international community.

"Georgia is a sovereign nation, and its territorial integrity must be respected," Bush said. "We have made clear to the Russian government that its actions this week are inconsistent with its relationship with the United States, with Europe, and with other countries in the world."

The conflict erupted over the weekend after Georgian forces launched an offensive to retake control of South Ossetia, a pro-Russian separatist region that has sought independence from Tbilisi since the early 1990s. Russia responded with a large-scale military counteroffensive, sending tanks and troops into South Ossetia and launching airstrikes on Georgian targets, including areas near the capital, Tbilisi.

Bush, who had cultivated a personal relationship with Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and championed Georgia's aspirations to join NATO, expressed strong support for the Georgian government while stopping short of announcing any direct military involvement.

"The United States calls on Russia to cease attacks on Georgia by aircraft and missiles, respect Georgia's territorial integrity, and withdraw its ground forces from Georgian soil," Bush said.

The president's remarks came after he attended the opening ceremonies of the Beijing Olympics, where he held brief discussions with Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin about the escalating crisis. Bush administration officials said the president urged Putin directly to de-escalate the conflict.

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice was dispatched to the region for consultations, and the administration signaled it was considering diplomatic and economic measures against Moscow if the fighting continued.

Critics, including some foreign policy analysts, questioned whether the U.S. had sufficient leverage to influence Russian actions, given American military commitments in Iraq and Afghanistan. Others noted the delicate balance the administration faced in supporting Georgia — a close ally and NATO aspirant — without provoking a larger confrontation with Moscow.

The White House said it was coordinating closely with European allies and the United Nations Security Council to seek a resolution to the crisis, though Russia's position as a permanent Security Council member complicated efforts to pass any binding measures.

As the fighting continued into a third day, humanitarian concerns mounted, with reports of civilian casualties and displacement in South Ossetia and surrounding Georgian territory. The Bush administration pledged humanitarian assistance and said it was monitoring the situation "very closely."

The crisis marked one of the most serious confrontations between Washington and Moscow since the end of the Cold War, raising fresh questions about the future of U.S.-Russia relations in the final months of the Bush presidency.

*CNN's coverage of this developing story will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# Global Powers Scramble as Georgia Conflict Threatens New Cold War Divide

**BEIJING/WASHINGTON/TBILISI** — The diplomatic fallout from Russia's military intervention in Georgia continued to reverberate across world capitals Tuesday, as President Bush, speaking from the Olympic Games in Beijing, issued his sharpest condemnation yet of Moscow's actions, warning that Russia's "disproportionate response" threatened to unravel decades of post-Cold War cooperation.

"Russia has invaded a sovereign neighboring state and threatens a democratic government elected by its people," Bush said in a statement delivered against the surreal backdrop of the Beijing Games, where he had traveled to support American athletes even as war raged thousands of miles away. "This is unacceptable in the 21st century."

The optics were impossible to ignore: an American president attending a global sporting spectacle hosted by an authoritarian government, while forced to respond in real time to a separate authoritarian power's tanks rolling through the Caucasus. Bush's aides described frantic behind-the-scenes consultations, phone calls with Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili, and coordination with European allies, all conducted between Olympic events.

## A Conflict Years in the Making

The fighting erupted after Georgian forces moved to reassert control over South Ossetia, a breakaway region that has functioned with de facto independence — and Russian backing — since the early 1990s. Moscow responded with overwhelming force, sending armored columns not only into South Ossetia but deeper into Georgian territory, and launching airstrikes that hit targets far from the immediate conflict zone.

Russian officials framed the operation as a "peace enforcement" mission necessary to protect Russian citizens and peacekeepers in South Ossetia, many of whom hold Russian passports issued in recent years — a policy Georgian officials have long called a pretext for annexation.

"What we are witnessing is naked aggression dressed up as humanitarian concern," one senior Georgian official told reporters in Tbilisi, as the capital braced for the possibility of further Russian advances.

## Washington's Delicate Balancing Act

For the Bush administration, the crisis lands at a particularly awkward moment. Georgia has been among Washington's closest allies in the former Soviet space, a vocal supporter of NATO expansion, and a contributor of troops to the Iraq war effort — troops the U.S. has since helped airlift home as the crisis intensified.

Yet the administration's options for a forceful response are constrained. With American military resources stretched thin across Iraq and Afghanistan, and with Russia holding permanent veto power on the U.N. Security Council, officials have been left to rely largely on diplomatic pressure and rhetorical condemnation.

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who has been in close contact with counterparts across Europe, is expected to travel to the region in the coming days. Vice President Cheney, in a sharply worded statement, said Russian "aggression must not go unanswered."

Critics, however, have questioned whether Washington's warnings carry real weight without a credible mechanism for enforcement — and whether years of American rhetoric encouraging Georgian aspirations toward NATO membership may have inadvertently emboldened Tbilisi into a confrontation it could not win.

## European Allies Divided on Response

The response from European capitals has been notably more cautious than Washington's, reflecting the continent's deep energy dependence on Russian oil and natural gas. French President Nicolas Sarkozy, holding the rotating presidency of the European Union, has taken the lead in shuttle diplomacy, working to broker a ceasefire framework between Moscow and Tbilisi.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel, whose country relies on Russian gas supplies for a substantial share of its energy needs, has called for de-escalation while stopping short of the harsher language emerging from Washington and London.

"There is no unified European position, and Moscow knows it," said one Western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity. "The Russians have calculated, probably correctly, that European economic interests will blunt any serious collective response."

## Russia Unmoved

In Moscow, officials showed little sign of backing down. Russian President Dmitry Medvedev defended the military operation as necessary and proportionate, while Prime Minister Vladimir Putin — who was also in Beijing for the Olympics opening ceremony when the conflict began, in a striking parallel to Bush's own presence — canceled his public schedule to return to direct crisis management from Moscow.

Putin, in blunt remarks to reporters, accused Georgia of initiating the violence and suggested Western nations bore some responsibility for emboldening Saakashvili's government.

## What Comes Next

As of Tuesday evening, questions remained about whether Russian forces would withdraw to pre-conflict positions or seek to consolidate control over disputed territories. Reports of Russian movements near the Georgian city of Gori, well outside South Ossetia proper, raised fears in Western capitals that Moscow's ambitions extended beyond the breakaway region itself.

For Bush, the crisis represents a bitter coda to a presidency that once declared, after his first meeting with Putin in 2001, that he had looked into the Russian leader's eyes and gotten "a sense of his soul." Seven years later, standing in Beijing, the American president's language carried none of that early optimism — replaced instead by blunt warnings about invasion, sovereignty, and the specter of renewed great-power confrontation.

Whether those warnings translate into meaningful consequences for Moscow remains, for now, an open question — one that will likely define the closing months of the Bush administration's foreign policy legacy.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

**WASHINGTON** — The brief but bloody war between Russia and Georgia in August 2008 has triggered the sharpest deterioration in U.S.-Russia relations since the Cold War, with American officials condemning what they call a disproportionate invasion while Moscow accuses Washington of hypocrisy and provocation.

## Background: A Frozen Conflict Reignites

The conflict centers on South Ossetia, a mountainous region in northern Georgia that has functioned as a de facto independent territory since a war in the early 1990s split it from Tbilisi's control. Most residents hold Russian passports, and Moscow has maintained "peacekeeping" troops there for over a decade under international agreements following the earlier conflict.

Tensions boiled over on August 7-8, when Georgian forces launched an offensive to retake the breakaway region's capital, Tskhinvali, after what Tbilisi described as escalating shelling from separatist forces. Russia responded with overwhelming military force, sending tanks and troops not only into South Ossetia but into undisputed Georgian territory, striking targets including the city of Gori and threatening the capital itself.

The five-day war left hundreds dead, displaced tens of thousands, and ended with a French-brokered ceasefire — though Russian forces remained in Georgian territory well beyond the agreed withdrawal timeline, prompting Western accusations that Moscow had exceeded any legitimate peacekeeping mandate.

## The Pipeline Factor

Analysts note the conflict carries significant energy implications. Georgia hosts the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, a critical Western-backed conduit that transports Caspian Sea oil to Turkey's Mediterranean coast while bypassing Russian territory entirely. The pipeline was built specifically to reduce European dependence on Russian energy infrastructure, and its proximity to the fighting — though not directly targeted — underscored Georgia's strategic importance in the broader contest over energy routes from Central Asia to European markets.

Critics of Russia's intervention argue Moscow's actions send an unmistakable signal to Western energy interests about the risks of bypassing Russian pipelines, while Russian officials have dismissed such characterizations as conspiratorial.

## Washington's Response

President George W. Bush condemned Russia's actions in blunt terms, declaring that "bullying and intimidation are not acceptable ways to conduct foreign policy in the 21st century" and demanding Russian forces withdraw immediately. The administration dispatched Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice to Tbilisi in a show of support for President Mikheil Saakashvili's government, and the U.S. Navy delivered humanitarian aid to Georgian ports — a move Moscow viewed as thinly veiled military signaling.

Vice President Dick Cheney was more combative, asserting that "Russian aggression must not go unanswered" and floating the possibility of reconsidering Russia's participation in international institutions, including the G8.

The presidential campaign trail reflected the crisis' political resonance. Republican nominee John McCain, invoking his long-standing hawkish stance toward Moscow, declared "we are all Georgians," while Democratic nominee Barack Obama called for restraint on both sides but similarly emphasized Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

## Moscow's Rebuttal

Russian President Dmitry Medvedev and Prime Minister Vladimir Putin dismissed Western criticism as hypocritical, drawing pointed comparisons to NATO's 1999 intervention in Kosovo — an operation Russia had long opposed — and to the U.S. invasion of Iraq. Putin, in particular, suggested American political considerations, including the U.S. election calendar, may have factored into Georgia's decision to attack South Ossetia, implying tacit U.S. encouragement of Saakashvili's move.

Russian officials framed their military response as a legitimate defense of Russian citizens and peacekeepers, comparing it to actions any government would take to protect its nationals from what they characterized as a Georgian assault amounting to genocide against South Ossetians.

## Broader Implications

The confrontation has reignited debate in Washington over NATO's eastward expansion, with Georgia's aspirations for alliance membership — publicly discussed at NATO's Bucharest summit just months earlier — now viewed by some analysts as a contributing factor to Moscow's assertiveness. Others argue the episode demonstrates precisely why Georgia and Ukraine require Western security guarantees.

European allies have shown less appetite for confrontation than Washington, with French President Nicolas Sarkozy brokering the ceasefire and several EU nations wary of jeopardizing energy relationships with Russia, which supplies substantial portions of the continent's natural gas.

As of this writing, Russian forces maintain checkpoints beyond South Ossetia's administrative boundaries, international monitors have been denied full access to affected areas, and the diplomatic standoff shows no signs of near-term resolution — leaving analysts to debate whether the conflict represents an isolated flashpoint or the opening chapter of a broader recalibration in East-West relations.

*This article reflects developments as reported through late August 2008.*
